description: A small weekly Esperanto word, a simple sentence, and the documented source material that Zamenhof reshaped into a regular planned language.
weather: Regular grammar, scattered accusatives, excellent chance of affixes.

entries.lede: A friend arrives wearing the dependable Esperanto noun ending -o and carrying a recognisably European root.

origin.note: Esperanto amik- belongs to the international Romance family represented by Latin amīcus and French ami; -o marks the noun.

sentence.note: Esperanto stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable. The present-tense ending -as does not change for person or number.

entries.source_note: Esperanto roots were often selected for international recognisability rather than copied mechanically from one language. The origin card names the clearest source family.

entries.lede: Aqua takes Esperanto’s regular noun ending and emerges as akvo, ready for drinking, rain, or an accusative -n.

origin.note: The root is modelled on Latin aqua and Romance descendants such as Italian acqua, adapted to Esperanto spelling and phonotactics.

sentence.note: The final -n marks the direct object. The noun itself remains the familiar akvo underneath.

entries.source_note: The route is an international learned/Romance comparison, not a claim that speakers borrowed the word in a single historical conversation.

entries.lede: The Germanic hound family becomes the everyday Esperanto word for any dog, not merely a hunting one.

origin.note: Esperanto hundo closely follows German Hund, with the regular Esperanto noun ending -o.

sentence.note: No indefinite article is needed; la is the definite article, and dormas is present tense.

entries.source_note: The German model is especially transparent, while cognates elsewhere in Germanic help explain why the root felt international.

entries.lede: English bird receives one extra vowel and the regular -o that tells every Esperantist it is a noun.

origin.note: Birdo is transparently modelled on English bird and adapted to Esperanto’s pronounce-every-letter pattern.

sentence.note: Esperanto has no indefinite article. Context supplies the natural English ‘a’.

entries.source_note: This is one of Esperanto’s unusually obvious English-looking roots; the morphological ending still makes it fully Esperanto.

entries.lede: Home and Heim meet in hejmo, which names home as a place or idea rather than merely a building.

origin.note: The root draws on the Germanic set represented by German Heim and English home; Esperanto writes j for the glide in hej.

sentence.note: The possessive mia agrees as an adjective, and ĉi tie means ‘here’.

entries.source_note: Several familiar Germanic forms converge here. The card therefore names a source family rather than insisting on a single donor.

entries.lede: A broadly Romance book word enters Esperanto almost unchanged and immediately becomes productive: librejo is a bookshop, libraro a collection.

origin.note: The form matches the Romance family descended from Latin liber, especially Italian and Spanish libro.

sentence.note: Esperanto present tense can cover English simple or progressive readings; libron carries the object ending -n.

entries.source_note: The same root can be recognisable in several source languages. Esperanto’s regular affixes then do work that those languages distribute less predictably.

entries.lede: French manger is regularised into manĝi, with the Esperanto infinitive ending -i and one letter, ĝ, doing the work of ‘j’ in judge.

origin.note: The root follows French manger; Esperanto ĝ represents /d͡ʒ/, while -i marks the infinitive.

sentence.note: Change infinitive -i to -as for present tense; panon is the direct object.

entries.source_note: The spelling is an adaptation, not a preserved French pronunciation. Esperanto maps the source-shaped root into its own regular sound system.

entries.lede: A Romance speaking root becomes paroli; from the same stem, parolo is a spoken word or speech and parole is adverbial.

origin.note: Parol- reflects Romance verbs such as Italian parlare and French parler, remodelled with Esperanto verb endings.

sentence.note: Language names can take the accusative when they are the object of paroli in this construction.

entries.source_note: The precise weighting of French and Italian models is less important than the visible Romance comparison; the Esperanto derivational system is its own.

entries.lede: English sun supplies a compact root; Esperanto makes suno, then builds sunny suna and sunlight sunlumo without irregularity.

origin.note: Suno is closely modelled on English sun, with -o marking the noun.

sentence.note: Brilas is the present tense of brili, ‘to shine’.

entries.source_note: The root later made another journey: Toki Pona borrowed its own suno from Esperanto.

entries.lede: Latin lūna and its Romance descendants give Esperanto a moon word that pairs neatly with suno.

origin.note: The form is shared across the Romance family and closely matches Latin lūna.

sentence.note: Adjectives end in -a; hela describes luno without an agreement surprise.

entries.source_note: A widely shared Romance form offered exactly the international recognisability Esperanto’s vocabulary selection often sought.

entries.lede: Bona is good in the broad, useful sense—and its root was recognisable enough to travel onward into Toki Pona as pona.

origin.note: The root aligns with Latin bonus and Romance forms such as Italian buona; -a is the Esperanto adjective ending.

sentence.note: Bona is predicative here. The same root makes bone, ‘well’, by changing -a to -e.

entries.source_note: The origin is best understood as a Romance internationalism. Its later borrowing into Toki Pona is documented separately on that site.

entries.lede: Bela gathers a familiar Romance beauty root and gives it the perfectly regular Esperanto adjective ending -a.

origin.note: The form compares closely with French belle and Italian bella, both ultimately related to Latin bellus.

sentence.note: The circumflex in ĝ represents /d͡ʒ/; the rest is pronounced as written.

entries.source_note: Esperanto’s source selection is multilingual. This card shows a comparison set and avoids declaring one modern language the exclusive parent.
